flagged.title: Act 2: The Boycott & Resistance
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims Odimba includes white allies like trade unionists (who historically enforced the colour bar) and depicts Margot developing cross-racial political solidarity with the boycott in Act 2, which would lose students marks in GCSE character and context questions.

mark_affecting.quote: Odimba intentionally complicates a simple Black versus white narrative by bringing in historically accurate white allies. The real boycott worked partly because of cross-racial support from university students, church groups, and progressive trade unionists.

At first she's super skeptical, but her evolution from resisting Wendell's ideas to showing grudging respect is huge. It represents the conflicted response of the white community, and gives the play this really powerful note of cross-racial solidarity.

flagged.title: Act 3: Resolution & Hope
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims Princess delivers a final speech/monologue directly addressing the audience at the end of the play, which would penalise GCSE students on drama/text knowledge.

mark_affecting.quote: she is speaking directly to the audience about the future... The play opens in Act 1 with Princess Candie directly addressing the audience, and it ends right here in Act 3 doing the exact same thing.

flagged.title: Character Analysis
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims that Odimba fills the stage with community characters who represent real-life historical figures like Paul Stephenson and Roy Hackett, when in reality there are only two non-family characters in the entire play and no historical boycott organisers appear on stage.

mark_affecting.quote: Odimba fills the stage with the neighbours and supporting characters of St. Paul's... and amazingly, they represent real-life historical figures, like Paul Stephenson and Roy Hackett, grounding the whole story in real history.

flagged.title: Structure, Staging & Language
flagged.reason: The video invents 'ensemble moments' and 'community scenes' punctuated throughout the play, directly contradicting the lesson text which explains the play uses a small cast of seven where the boycott only arrives as news into the home.

mark_affecting.video_says: Finally, there are ensemble moments. The tight family drama is periodically punctuated by community scenes, kind of zooming the camera out to show the family's struggles within the wider social context of St Paul's.
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Small cast: Only seven characters appear. The boycott arrives as news carried into the flat, which keeps the play’s scope intimate.

flagged.title: Key Themes
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims Odimba includes white allies (students, church members, workers) supporting the boycott in the play, whereas the play features only one white character (Margot), who explicitly refuses to support the boycott.

mark_affecting.video_says: Odimba deliberately includes white allies: students, church members, workers, supporting the boycott, but she handles this incredibly carefully.
mark_affecting.lesson_says: The only white character is Margot, who will not support the boycott but does shelter Princess when she runs away... The one white character is present but never centred.
